# Overview of fungal infections

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Infectious lung diseases > Overview of fungal infections*

[Original Article Link](/library/EF08P3)

---

## Summary

Fungal infections are categorized by the anatomical location of the infection (i.e., as <u>superficial</u> or systemic) and the epidemiological class of the infecting organism (i.e., <u>endemic fungal infection</u> or <u>opportunistic fungal infection</u>). Infections in immunocompetent individuals are generally <u>superficial</u> or limited to the respiratory system. <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u> are susceptible to <u>systemic fungal infections</u>, which are associated with a high risk of mortality. Diagnosing a <u>systemic fungal infection</u> is often difficult because the symptoms are nonspecific and definitive test results may take days to weeks. Suspected <u>systemic fungal infections</u> are usually treated empirically until <u>confirmatory testing</u> is obtained.




See also “<u>General mycology</u>,” “<u>Candidiasis</u>,” “<u>Aspergillosis</u>,” and “<u>Dermatophyte infections</u>.”

---

## Superficial fungal infections

* <u>Superficial fungal infection</u>: fungal infection limited to <u>skin</u>, <u>hair</u>, <u>nails</u>, <u>superficial</u> mucus membranes, and <u>subcutaneous tissue</u>, without involvement of internal organs

* Dermatomycoses: mycotic infections of tissue with high <u>keratin</u> content (<u>skin</u>, <u>nails</u>, <u>hair</u>) caused mainly by <u>dermatophytes</u>, but may also result from <u>opportunistic infection</u> with other species of fungus (e.g., Malassezia).

## Systemic fungal infections

* Definition

* Fungal infections that affect internal organs of the body and are not confined to <u>skin</u>, subcutaneous tissues, or mucus membranes.

* Fungemia: the presence of a fungus in the bloodstream

* Etiology

* <u>Opportunistic infections</u>: affects <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> (see “<u>Opportunistic fungal infections</u>”)

* <u>Endemic disease</u>: affects both immunocompetent and <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> (see “<u>Endemic fungal infections</u>”)

---

## Opportunistic fungal infections

| <u>Aspergillosis</u> | <br><br>* <u>Aspergillus fumigatus</u><br><br>* <u>Aspergillus flavus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Immunocompromise</u><br><br>* Chronic granulomatous infection<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ABPA</u><br><br>* Associated with <u>asthma</u> and <u>cystic fibrosis</u><br><br>* Causes <u>bronchiectasis</u> and <u>eosinophilia</u><br><br>* Pulmonary <u>aspergilloma</u>: <u>chronic cough</u>, <u>hemoptysis</u><br><br>* <u>Invasive aspergillosis</u>: <u>fever</u>, <u>cough</u>, <u>respiratory distress</u><br><br>* <u>Endocarditis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ABPA</u><br><br>* <u>Eosinophilia</u><br><br>* Elevated <u>IgE</u> levels<br><br>* Pulmonary infiltrates on chest <u>x-ray</u> or CT<br><br>* Pulmonary <u>aspergilloma</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u> or CT shows mobile fungus ball<br><br>* <u>Serology</u> is positive for <u>Aspergillus</u> <u>IgG</u><br><br>* <u>Invasive aspergillosis</u>: tissue <u>biopsy</u> showing 45° angle branching septate <u>hyphae</u> with fruiting bodies<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ABPA</u><br><br>* Oral <u>prednisone</u> for severe cases<br><br>* <u>Itraconazole</u> for recurrent episodes<br><br>* Pulmonary <u>aspergilloma</u>: <u>lobectomy</u> for <u>massive hemoptysis</u><br><br>* <u>Invasive aspergillosis</u>: IV <u>voriconazole</u>, <u>caspofungin</u>, OR <u>amphotericin B</u><br><br><br> |
| Invasive <u>candidiasis</u> | <br>* <u>Candida albicans</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)<br><br>* Medications (<u>antibiotics</u>, <u>steroids</u>, cytostatic agents, <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>)<br><br>* Hematologic malignancies (e.g., <u>acute myeloid leukemia</u>, <u>multiple myeloma</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Candida esophagitis</u><br><br>* <u>Systemic candidiasis</u><br><br>* General: e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>sepsis</u>, <u>myalgias</u><br><br>* Organ infiltration: e.g., multiple <u>abscesses</u>, <u>endocarditis</u>, <u>meningitis</u>, pulmonary <u>candidiasis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Best initial: <u>KOH test</u> showing <u>budding</u> <u>yeasts</u> and <u>pseudohyphae</u> at 20Â°C<br><br>* Confirmatory: fungal <u>blood culture</u> or tissue <u>biopsy</u><br><br>* <u>AIDS-defining condition</u> if <u>esophagus</u>, <u>trachea</u>, <u>bronchi</u>, or <u>lung parenchyma</u> are involved<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Candida esophagitis</u>: oral or IV <u>fluconazole</u><br><br>* <u>Systemic candidiasis</u>: IV <u>echinocandins</u> (e.g., <u>caspofungin</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Cryptococcosis | <br>* Cryptococcus neoformans<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>AIDS</u><br><br>* Exposure to pigeon droppings/soil<br><br>* Transmission via inhalation<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis</u> or <u>brain abscess</u><br><br>* Hematogenous spread of fungi to <u>meninges</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>signs of increased intracranial pressure</u>, confusion, absent <u>meningeal signs</u><br><br>* Pulmonary cryptococcosis<br><br>* Most commonly seen in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients<br><br>* Clinical presentation is variable and nonspecific (e.g., <u>cough</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>shortness of breath</u>).<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Latex agglutination test</u>: positive for <u>cryptococcal</u> <u>polysaccharide</u> capsular <u>antigen</u><br><br>* High <u>specificity</u> and <u>sensitivity</u><br><br>* Specimen: Blood or <u>CSF</u><br><br>* <u>CSF analysis</u><br><br>* <u>India ink stain</u>: clear halo<br><br>* <u>Mucicarmine</u>: stains the thick inner <u>polysaccharide</u> capsule bright red<br><br>* Fungal culture (<u>Sabouraud agar</u>) showing:<br><br>* 5–10 μm <u>yeast</u><br><br>* Thick <u>polysaccharide</u> capsule<br><br>* Narrow, unequal <u>budding</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: “Soap bubble” lesions in <u>cryptococcal</u> <u>encephalitis</u> .[[4]](/library/3UbS1G)<br><br>* <u>AIDS-defining condition</u> if extrapulmonary<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cryptococcal meningitis</u><br><br>* IV <u>amphotericin B</u> PLUS <u>flucytosine</u> followed by oral <u>fluconazole</u><br><br>* <u>Maintenance therapy</u>: oral <u>fluconazole</u> (until symptoms resolve and <u>CD4</u> > 100/mmÂ³ for at least 1 year)<br><br>* Serial therapeutic LPs for <u>increased intracranial pressure</u><br><br> |
| <u>Pneumocystis pneumonia</u> | <br>* <u>P. jirovecii</u> (previously <u>P. carinii</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (especially if <u>CD4 count</u> < 200/mmÂ³)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Fever</u>, <u>exertional dyspnea</u>, nonproductive <u>cough</u>, weight loss, impaired oxygenation<br><br> | <br><br>* CT: diffuse, bilateral <u>ground-glass opacities</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: bilateral opacities<br><br>* <u>Bronchoalveolar lavage</u> or <u>lung</u> <u>biopsy</u> (if <u>sputum</u> is negative): <u>silver stain</u> and <u>immunofluorescence</u> show disc-shaped <u>yeasts</u><br><br>* <u>AIDS-defining condition</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* High-dose <u>TMP-SMX</u> (treatment and prophylaxis) OR <u>dapsone</u> with/without <u>pyrimethamine</u><br><br>* <u>Prednisone</u> (moderate to severe <u>hypoxemia</u>)<br><br>* Prophylaxis: <u>CD4</u> < 200/mmÂ³<br><br><br> |
| <br>Mucormycosis  <br> | <br>* Zygomycetes Mucor and Rhizopus (e.g., <u>Rhizopus oryzae</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Diabetes</u>, particularly with ketoacidosis<br><br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u><br><br>* <u>Chronic sinusitis</u> (> 3 months)<br><br>* <u>Iron overload</u> or treatment with <u>deferoxamine</u><br><br>* Major trauma [[5]](/library/Qt1uWi0)<br><br>* <u>Burns</u> [[5]](/library/Qt1uWi0)<br><br>* <u>COVID-19</u> infection [[6]](/library/jt1_Wi0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Invasive <u>chronic sinusitis</u> and <u>orbital cellulitis</u><br><br>* May lead to tissue <u>necrosis</u> and contiguous spread to the <u>orbit</u>, <u>brain</u>, and <u>palate</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u>, facial <u>pain</u><br><br>* Black <u>necrotic</u> <u>eschar</u> on face and/or <u>palate</u><br><br>* Possible <u>cranial nerve</u> involvement<br><br>* Rhinocerebral, <u>frontal lobe</u> <u>abscess</u><br><br>* <u>Cavernous sinus thrombosis</u><br><br>* Pulmonary <u>mucormycosis</u>: aggressive infection of the bronchioli and <u>alveoli</u>, manifesting with <u>fever</u> and <u>hemoptysis</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebritis</u>, <u>mediastinitis</u>, cardiac involvement in severe cases<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Imaging<br><br>* Assess the extent of tissue damage and organ involvement<br><br>* Head CT: <u>sinusitis</u> with orbital and intracranial involvement<br><br>* Tissue <u>biopsy</u> (confirmatory): wide-angled branching of irregularly shaped, broad, nonseptate <u>hyphae</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Surgical debridement</u><br><br>* IV <u>amphotericin B</u> OR <u>isavuconazole</u><br><br>* Elimination of <u>risk factors</u>, aggressive blood <u>glucose</u> control<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Candida</u>, <u>Aspergillus</u>, and <u>Cryptococcus</u> are opportunistic fungal pathogens with low inherent <u>virulence</u>. They commonly cause systemic mycoses in <u>immunocompromised</u> hosts but do not normally affect healthy hosts.

## Endemic fungal infections

* Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>dimorphic fungi</u>

* No interpersonal transmission

* Clinical features: : <u>pneumonia</u>, disseminated systemic infection





| Overview of the most common <u>endemic fungal infections</u> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Pathogen</u> | <u>Risk factors</u> | Clinical features | Diagnostics | Treatment |
| Histoplasmosis | <br>* Histoplasma capsulatum<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Endemic</u> areas: Mississippi and the Ohio river valley<br><br>* Exposure to bird or bat droppings in <u>endemic</u> areas through activities such as spelunking (cave exploration)<br><br>* <u>Immunosuppression</u> (e.g., <u>AIDS</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Often asymptomatic<br><br>* <u>Flulike</u> illness: <u>fever</u>, weight loss, <u>erythema nodosum</u>, <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>, <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, nonproductive <u>cough</u><br><br>* Ulcerative oral lesion (palatal, <u>tongue</u> <u>ulcers</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u>: diffuse nodular densities, focal infiltrate or cavity, or <u>lymphadenopathy</u><br><br>* Best initial: positive urine and serum <u>polysaccharide</u> <u>antigen</u> test<br><br>* <u>Silver stain</u> of <u>biopsy</u> or <u>bronchoalveolar lavage</u> showing <br><br>* <u>Macrophages</u> filled with <u>yeast</u> cells that measure 1–5 μm and bud from a narrow base<br><br>* Fungi are identified by comparing their size to that of an <u>RBC</u> (fungal size < <u>RBC</u>)<br><br>* Culture (blood, <u>sputum</u>, <u>bone marrow</u>, <u>lymph node</u>, <u>liver</u>): <u>Sabouraud agar</u><br><br>* <u>Liver biopsy</u>: demonstrates disseminated disease with the presence of fungal organisms in the <u>yeast</u>-stage of development<br><br>* <u>CBC</u>: <u>eosinophilia</u>, <u>pancytopenia</u> (disseminated disease)<br><br>* <u>AIDS-defining</u> illness if disseminated or extrapulmonary<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mild disease: supportive therapy<br><br>* Chronic cavitation: oral <u>itraconazole</u> > 1 year<br><br>* Severe pulmonary or disseminated disease: IV <u>amphotericin B</u>/liposomal then oral <u>itraconazole</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Coccidioidomycosis (<u>valley fever</u>) | <br><br>* Coccidioides immitis<br><br>* Coccidioides posadasii<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Travel to Southwestern United States, California<br><br>* Soil/dust exposure in <u>endemic</u> areas (e.g., during windstorms, earthquakes, archeological explorations) [[7]](/library/HfbKnG)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Flu-like</u> illness or <u>pneumonia</u>: <u>fever</u>, <u>cough</u>, night sweats, <u>anorexia</u>, <u>chest pain</u>, and <u>dyspnea</u><br><br>* Extrapulmonary findings<br><br>* <u>CNS</u>: <u>meningitis</u><br><br>* <u>Skin</u>: <u>erythema nodosum</u> (desert bumps)<br><br>* <u>Joints</u>: <u>arthralgia</u> (desert rheumatism)<br><br>* Bone: multiple <u>osteolytic lesions</u> [[8]](/library/SoXyY_)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Serology</u><br><br>* Increased <u>IgM</u> (increases within 2 weeks of infection and disappears after 2 months)<br><br>* Increased <u>IgG</u> at 1–3 months<br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u>: normal or infiltrates/<u>lymphadenopathy</u>/<u>pleural effusion</u><br><br>* KOH, <u>silver stain</u>, or culture (<u>sputum</u>, wound <u>exudate</u>, <u>joint effusion</u>) showing<br><br>* Large spherules containing <u>endospores</u><br><br>* Fungi are identified by comparing their size to that of an <u>RBC</u> (fungal size > <u>RBC</u>)<br><br>* <u>CBC</u>: <u>eosinophilia</u><br><br>* <u>AIDS-defining</u> illness if disseminated or extrapulmonary<br><br><br> | <br><br>* IV <u>amphotericin B</u> (severe infection)<br><br>* Alternative: <u>itraconazole</u><br><br><br> |
| Paracoccidioidomycosis | <br>* Paracoccidioides species<br><br>* Paracoccidioides brasiliensis<br><br>* Paracoccidioides lutzii<br><br> | <br><br>* Travel to South and Central America<br><br>* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>  [[9]](/library/RUbl1G)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Infected patients often asymptomatic<br><br>* Painful nasal, pharyngeal, and laryngeal <u>mucosal</u> <u>ulcerations</u><br><br>* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u> (usually cervical)<br><br>* Can disseminate → extrapulmonary manifestations (e.g., <u>verrucous</u> <u>skin</u> lesions similar to those of cutaneous <u>blastomycosis</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* KOH/calcofluor staining on smears or silver/<u>PAS</u>-staining on tissue <u>biopsy</u><br><br>* <u>Budding</u> <u>yeast</u> with “captain's wheel” formation<br><br>* Fungi are identified by comparing their size to that of an <u>RBC</u> (fungal size > <u>RBC</u>)<br><br>* Cultures have low <u>sensitivity</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Itraconazole</u><br><br>* Severe or refractory cases: <u>amphotericin B</u><br><br><br> |
| Blastomycosis | <br>* Blastomyces dermatitidis<br><br> | <br>* Travel to Southeastern, Central, Eastern, and the Great Lakes region of the United States<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pneumonia</u><br><br>* Extrapulmonary findings<br><br>* <u>Skin</u>: <u>verrucous</u> lesions and granulomatous <u>nodules</u> (lesions resemble <u>squamous cell cancer</u>)<br><br>* Bone: <u>osteolytic lesions</u> (most commonly in the <u>ribs</u>, <u>vertebrae</u>, and <u>long bones</u>) [[10]](/library/sfbtnG)<br><br>* Genitourinary involvement: <u>prostatitis</u>, <u>orchitis</u>, <u>epididymitis</u><br><br>* <u>CNS</u> lesions: <u>meningitis</u>, epidural/intracranial <u>abscesses</u><br><br><br> | <br>* KOH or culture (confirmatory) of <u>sputum</u>, urine, or body fluids showing:<br><br>* <u>Yeast</u> form (at body temperature or > 37Â°C): broad-based buds<br><br>* Fungi are identified by comparing their size to that of an <u>RBC</u> (fungal size ≈ <u>RBC</u>)<br><br>* <u>Mold</u> form (at room temperature): circular fungal cells with filamentous <u>hyphae</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Local infection: <u>fluconazole</u> and <u>itraconazole</u><br><br>* Systemic infection: IV <u>amphotericin B</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> “History of the hidden Ohio and Mississippi river valleys:” Histoplasma is hidden within <u>macrophages</u> and Ohio and Mississippi river valleys are the <u>endemic</u> regions of <u>histoplasma</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> “Paracoccidiomycosis steers the ship to South and Central America at the captain's wheel: ”Paracoccidiomycosis is <u>endemic</u> in South and Central America and its <u>budding</u> <u>yeast</u> has a captain's wheel appearance.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>yeast</u> form of Blastomycosis forms broad-based buds.




> [!TIP]
> Unlike most other <u>dimorphic fungi</u>, <u>Blastomyces</u> can cause disseminated disease even in immunocompetent hosts.

## Other fungal infections

See also “<u>Mycetoma</u>.”




### Sporotrichosis (<u>rose gardener disease</u>)




* Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>: Sporothrix schenckii (a <u>dimorphic fungus</u> that feeds on decaying vegetation)

* <u>Risk factor</u>: traumatic injury to the <u>skin</u> while gardening (e.g., thorn prick)

* Clinical features

* <u>Pustules</u> and <u>ulcers</u> with ascending <u>lymphangitis</u>

* <u>Nodules</u> along draining <u>lymphatics</u>

* Disseminated disease (in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients): <u>pneumonia</u>, <u>meningitis</u>

* Diagnostics

* Fungal culture;  (<u>sputum</u>, <u>pus</u>, <u>biopsy</u> tissue) showing dimorphic, cigar-shaped <u>yeast</u> (this form exists in humans)

* Septate <u>hyphae</u>, rosette-like <u>clusters</u> of <u>conidia</u> at the tips of the conidiophores (this form exists in soil/vegetation)

* Treatment [[11]](/library/JQ1sCg0)

* Cutaneous or lymphocutaneous

* First-line: <u>itraconazole</u> DOSAGE  [[11]](/library/JQ1sCg0)

* Alternative: <u>saturated solution of potassium iodide</u>

* Disseminated: <u>amphotericin B</u> DOSAGE [[11]](/library/JQ1sCg0)





> [!NOTE]
> “A rose gardener plants roses in a pot while smoking a cigar:” <u>sporotrichosis</u> is associated with traumatic gardening injuries, treatment includes potassium iodide, and <u>Sporothrix</u> appears as a cigar-shaped <u>yeast</u> in culture.

## Diagnosis

### Direct microscopy [[12]](/library/bRYHlK)




* Evaluation of <u>fungal morphology</u>

* Usually a KOH test is performed. [[1]](/library/iTdJq60)

* A sample of affected <u>skin</u>, <u>hair</u>, or <u>nail</u> tissue is placed onto a microscopy slide.

* 10–20% KOH solution is added, which dissolves <u>keratinocytes</u> but leaves fungal elements visible. [[13]](/library/VgYG8o)[[14]](/library/VSdGA60)

* A fungal stain  may be added to highlight fungal elements on microscopy. [[15]](/library/eSdxA60)

* Used for preliminary identification





### Wood lamp examination [[12]](/library/bRYHlK)




* A diagnostic test that employs a UV lamp to examine <u>skin</u> lesions

* Used to evaluate <u>superficial</u> <u>fungal infections of the skin</u> (e.g., <u>pityriasis versicolor</u>), which appear characteristically yellow-green fluorescent under <u>ultraviolet light</u>

* Can also be used to evaluate <u>hypopigmented</u> or depigmented lesions (e.g., <u>vitiligo</u>) which appear blue-white fluorescent





### Fungal culture [[12]](/library/bRYHlK)




* Fungal growth usually takes from 24–72 hours.

* Sabouraud agar: a fungal growth medium that contains dextrose and peptones (e.g., for the cultivation of <u>dermatophytes</u>, <u>Blastomyces</u>, <u>Histoplasma</u>, <u>Coccidioides</u>)

* Selective media: e.g., inhibitory <u>mold</u> agar and <u>dermatophyte</u> test media





### <u>Histological stains</u> [[12]](/library/bRYHlK)




* <u>Silver stain</u>

* <u>PAS</u> stain

* India ink stain: a type of negative stain with carbon that is most commonly used to identify organisms with a <u>polysaccharide</u> capsule such as <u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u> (the capsule is not penetrated by the ink and appears as a halo around the organism against a dark background)

* Mucicarmine: a staining method used to identify the thick <u>polysaccharide</u> capsule of some organisms (e.g., <u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u>, <u>Blastomyces dermatitidis</u>, <u>Coccidioides immitis</u>) and <u>mucin</u> (e.g., in gastric tumors); <u>mucicarmine stains</u> bright red





### Others [[12]](/library/bRYHlK)




* <u>Immunohistochemistry</u>: uses <u>antibodies</u> that bind to species-specific fungal <u>antigens</u>

* <u>Serologic studies</u> for <u>antibody</u> and <u>antigen</u> detection (e.g., <u>ELISA</u>, RIA, <u>latex agglutination assay</u>)

* <u>PCR</u> amplification of fungal <u>DNA</u>
